items.text: Bupropion：Norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake inhibitor（NDRI）；也拮抗nicotinic受器。
用於：憂鬱症、戒菸；與naltrexone合用減重。
考點：少性功能障礙、可減重/戒菸；但會癲癇。
常考/禁忌：失眠、口乾、焦慮、血壓上升；降低癲癇閾值，飲食疾患禁用。

statements.text: Bupropion is an aminoketone antidepressant; its antidepressant mechanism is not fully defined, but it inhibits neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine and does not inhibit monoamine oxidase.
Its smoking-cessation effect is presumed to involve noradrenergic and dopaminergic mechanisms rather than direct nicotine-receptor agonism.
Bupropion has dose-related seizure risk and can increase blood pressure; gradual titration and dose limits are central safety controls.
Sustained-release bupropion treats major depressive disorder.
A separately labeled sustained-release bupropion product is used as an aid to smoking cessation.
statements.scope: Smoking-cessation product; not interchangeable dosing by implication

statements.text: Treatment of major depressive disorder in adults.
Aid to smoking cessation treatment.
Common reactions include headache, dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, dizziness, constipation, agitation, anxiety, tremor, sweating, and anorexia.
Serious risks include dose-related seizure, hypertension, activation of mania or hypomania, psychosis, severe hypersensitivity, and suicidal thoughts or behaviors in younger patients.
False-positive urine immunoassay results for amphetamines can occur.
Boxed warning: antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults; monitor for clinical worsening and suicidality.

Contraindications include seizure disorder, current or prior bulimia or anorexia nervosa, abrupt discontinuation of alcohol or sedative/antiepileptic drugs, MAOI use within the prohibited interval, duplicate bupropion-containing therapy, and hypersensitivity.
Screen for bipolar disorder, monitor mood and behavior, and discontinue if a seizure occurs.
Smoking-cessation use requires monitoring for serious neuropsychiatric symptoms and suicidality even in patients without prior psychiatric disease.
Bupropion-associated pupillary dilation can precipitate an angle-closure attack in a patient with untreated anatomically narrow angles.
The mean elimination half-life of bupropion after chronic dosing is approximately 21 hours, while active metabolites persist longer.
Bupropion is extensively metabolized, including CYP2B6 formation of hydroxybupropion, and bupropion plus metabolites inhibit CYP2D6.
Bupropion and its metabolites are eliminated mainly in urine; accumulation can increase with renal impairment.
Bupropion inhibits CYP2D6 and may raise concentrations of selected antidepressants, antipsychotics, beta-blockers, and class Ic antiarrhythmics.
CYP2B6 inducers or inhibitors, dopaminergic drugs, MAOIs, alcohol, and drugs that lower seizure threshold require specific risk assessment.
Bupropion may decrease plasma digoxin concentrations; monitor digoxin concentrations during concomitant treatment.
Monitor blood pressure before and during treatment, psychiatric status and suicidality, emergence of mania, seizure risk factors, and smoking-cessation neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Consider reducing dose and/or frequency in renal impairment because bupropion and metabolites may accumulate.
Dose and frequency must be reduced in hepatic impairment according to Child-Pugh severity.
Safety and effectiveness of the reviewed single-agent SR formulation have not been established in pediatric patients.
Overdose can cause seizures, hallucinations, loss of consciousness, tachycardia, conduction disturbances, arrhythmias, and death; management is supportive with airway and ECG monitoring.
Exam distinction: bupropion is a norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake inhibitor used for depression and smoking cessation; seizure risk rises with dose and predisposing factors.
Do not convert the existence of naltrexone/bupropion into an approved single-agent bupropion weight-loss indication.

items.text: Deferasirox：口服鐵螯合劑：結合多餘鐵並促進排出。
慢性輸血鐵過載或非輸血性鐵過載（依藥物）。
考點：口服鐵螯合；deferiprone怕粒細胞缺乏。
常考/禁忌：腎/肝毒性、GI不適；deferiprone可顆粒球缺乏，deferasirox腎傷害。

mnemonics.text: p.125: 不一樣的鐵(defer)打針會喊

statements.text: Deferasirox is an orally active tridentate chelator with high selectivity for ferric iron; two molecules bind one iron atom and the chelated complex is excreted predominantly in feces.
Daily administration promotes net iron excretion; excessive dosing relative to iron burden can produce overchelation toxicity.
By lowering total body iron, deferasirox manages chronic iron overload from repeated transfusions or qualifying non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia.
Treatment of chronic iron overload due to blood transfusions in patients 2 years of age and older.
Treatment of chronic iron overload in patients 10 years of age and older with non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia syndromes when liver iron concentration and ferritin meet label thresholds.
Common adverse reactions include diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain, skin rash, and increases in serum creatinine.

Serious toxicities include acute kidney injury or renal failure, hepatic injury or failure, gastrointestinal hemorrhage or perforation, severe cytopenias, severe cutaneous reactions, and hypersensitivity.
Auditory and ocular disturbances can occur and require baseline and periodic assessment.
Boxed warning: deferasirox can cause renal failure, hepatic failure, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage, including fatal events; close laboratory and clinical monitoring is required.

Contraindications include estimated GFR below 40 mL/min/1.73 m², poor performance status, high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome, advanced malignancy, platelet count below 50 × 10⁹/L, or hypersensitivity.
Interrupt, reduce, or discontinue treatment for worsening renal or hepatic function, cytopenias, severe skin reactions, significant gastrointestinal injury, or suspected overchelation.
Volume depletion, nephrotoxic drugs, and acute illness increase renal toxicity risk, particularly in children.
The mean elimination half-life is generally in the range of about 8 to 16 hours.
Deferasirox undergoes mainly glucuronidation, especially through UGT1A1 and UGT1A3, with enterohepatic recycling.
Deferasirox and metabolites are excreted primarily in feces, with only a minor urinary contribution.
Concomitant anticoagulants, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or bisphosphonates can increase gastrointestinal ulceration or hemorrhage risk.
Do not take deferasirox with aluminum-containing antacid preparations.
Deferasirox may induce CYP3A4 and reduce concentrations of CYP3A4 substrates; monitor for reduced effectiveness of the concomitant substrate.
Deferasirox inhibits CYP2C8 and increases repaglinide exposure; consider reducing the repaglinide dose and monitor blood glucose carefully.

Deferasirox inhibits CYP1A2 and can increase theophylline exposure; avoid theophylline and other narrow-therapeutic-index CYP1A2 substrates when possible, or monitor concentrations and toxicity closely.
Strong UGT inducers can lower deferasirox exposure and efficacy; avoid them when possible or follow the label's dose-adjustment and response-monitoring instructions.
Bile-acid sequestrants can lower deferasirox exposure; avoid concomitant use when possible or follow the label's dose-adjustment and response-monitoring instructions.
Deferasirox increases busulfan exposure; monitor busulfan plasma concentrations and adjust the busulfan dose as needed.
Before treatment assess eGFR in duplicate, urinalysis and tubular function, liver tests, CBC, ferritin, and auditory and ophthalmic status.
During treatment monitor renal and hepatic function at label-specified intervals, CBC, monthly ferritin, and annual hearing and eye examinations; adjust for falling iron burden.
Do not use when eGFR is below 40 mL/min/1.73 m²; reduce the starting dose and intensify monitoring for lesser renal impairment according to the label.
Avoid severe hepatic impairment and reduce the starting dose in moderate hepatic impairment.
Pediatric use is indication- and age-specific; growth, renal function, and volume status need close surveillance.
Acute overdose has produced gastrointestinal symptoms and hepatic or renal injury; discontinue, provide supportive care, and monitor organ function and iron burden.
Deferasirox is an oral iron chelator; distinguish it from parenteral deferoxamine.
The central safety triad is kidney, liver, and gastrointestinal bleeding, with dose adjustment guided by iron burden and toxicity.
The safety and efficacy of deferasirox given with another iron-chelation therapy have not been established.

items.text: Denosumab：靶點：RANKL。機轉：單株抗體結合 RANKL → RANK 無法活化破骨細胞前驅細胞 → 破骨細胞形成/活性下降 → 骨吸收下降。
用於：骨質疏鬆、癌症骨轉移骨相關事件預防、巨大細胞骨腫瘤、高血鈣（依劑型/適應症）。
一句話：Denosumab = anti-RANKL，直接關掉破骨細胞。
常考：低血鈣、顎骨壞死、非典型股骨骨折、感染/皮膚反應；停藥反彈性椎體骨折；使用前補鈣/維生素D。

mnemonics.text: p.73: 唸起來像dinosaur，因為小行星砸下來死光了，所以被排在rank L，代表他們是 loser

statements.text: Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds RANK ligand, preventing RANK activation on osteoclasts and their precursors and thereby reducing osteoclast formation, function, and survival.
RANKL inhibition rapidly suppresses bone-resorption markers; the effect reverses after drug discontinuation rather than being retained in bone like a bisphosphonate.
PROLIA increases bone mass and reduces fracture risk in labeled osteoporosis and treatment-associated bone-loss populations.
XGEVA reduces skeletal complications in cancer-related bone disease and treats selected giant-cell tumor or refractory hypercalcemia settings.

PROLIA is indicated for several high-fracture-risk osteoporosis and therapy-associated bone-loss populations, including postmenopausal women, men, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, androgen-deprivation therapy, and aromatase-inhibitor therapy as specified by the label.

XGEVA is indicated for prevention of skeletal-related events in multiple myeloma and bone metastases from solid tumors, giant cell tumor of bone in defined patients, and hypercalcemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonate therapy.
Common PROLIA reactions vary by indication and include back or musculoskeletal pain, pain in extremity, hypercholesterolemia, and cystitis.
Common XGEVA reactions include fatigue/asthenia, hypophosphatemia, nausea, dyspnea, diarrhea, and headache depending on the oncology population.
Serious risks shared by the reviewed denosumab products include severe hypocalcemia, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture, and clinically significant hypersensitivity.
statements.scope: Risks shared by PROLIA and XGEVA

statements.text: PROLIA additionally carries warnings for serious infections requiring hospitalization and severe dermatologic reactions.
Stopping or substantially delaying PROLIA can cause rapid bone turnover and multiple vertebral fractures; transition to another antiresorptive therapy should be planned.
PROLIA boxed warning: severe hypocalcemia, including fatal cases, is increased in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease, especially with chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder.
Pre-existing hypocalcemia and hypersensitivity are contraindications; PROLIA is also contraindicated in pregnancy.
XGEVA is contraindicated in patients with pre-existing hypocalcemia and in those with known clinically significant hypersensitivity to XGEVA or denosumab products.
Correct hypocalcemia before treatment, provide calcium and vitamin D, and assess advanced CKD patients for CKD-MBD before PROLIA.
Perform an oral examination before therapy and avoid unnecessary invasive dental procedures because of osteonecrosis-of-jaw risk.
Do not administer PROLIA and XGEVA concomitantly because they contain the same active ingredient.
After a 60 mg subcutaneous dose, denosumab concentrations decline over months with a mean half-life of approximately 25 days.

In a study across degrees of renal function, including dialysis, renal impairment did not affect denosumab pharmacokinetics and no renal dose adjustment was necessary; advanced chronic kidney disease nevertheless markedly increases severe hypocalcemia risk.

In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, a 60 mg denosumab dose did not alter midazolam pharmacokinetics, indicating that CYP3A4-substrate pharmacokinetics are not expected to be altered in that population.
Do not administer denosumab-containing products concurrently; calcimimetics and other calcium-lowering drugs can further increase hypocalcemia risk and require closer calcium monitoring.

For PROLIA, correct hypocalcemia and ensure calcium and vitamin D supplementation; in susceptible patients without advanced CKD, check calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium 10 to 14 days after injection.

Before PROLIA in advanced CKD, evaluate CKD-MBD with the specified calcium, vitamin D, and parathyroid-hormone testing and consider assessing bone-turnover status; monitor serum calcium weekly for the first month after injection and monthly thereafter.
For XGEVA, monitor calcium throughout treatment, especially during the first weeks, and administer calcium, magnesium, and vitamin D as necessary.

For either denosumab product, monitor oral health and symptoms of osteonecrosis of the jaw and evaluate new thigh or groin pain; PROLIA patients should also be assessed for serious infection and severe dermatologic reactions.
For PROLIA, ensure the next 6-month dose is not missed without an alternative antiresorptive plan.
Denosumab can cause fetal harm; PROLIA is contraindicated in pregnancy and XGEVA labeling requires pregnancy risk counseling and contraception.
No dose adjustment is required solely for renal impairment, but advanced CKD greatly increases severe hypocalcemia risk and requires specialized evaluation and monitoring.
There is limited overdose experience; management centers on monitoring for exaggerated pharmacologic effects such as hypocalcemia and providing supportive care.
Denosumab targets RANKL, not RANK, and suppresses osteoclast development and activity.
Product separation is essential: PROLIA is 60 mg every 6 months for bone-loss indications, whereas XGEVA uses oncology-specific 120 mg schedules.

用於：GERD、胃/十二指腸潰瘍、胃酸過多、stress ulcer prophylaxis。
考點：H2 blocker抑酸比PPI弱；cimetidine最會CYP交互作用/抗androgen。
常考/禁忌：頭痛、腹瀉/便祕、老人譫妄；cimetidine：男性女乳、性功能障礙、CYP抑制。

statements.text: Famotidine competitively inhibits histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion and acid concentration.
Famotidine suppresses basal, nocturnal, and stimulated gastric acid secretion and reduces pepsin output as a consequence of lower gastric volume.
Acid suppression promotes healing and symptom control in labeled ulcer, gastroesophageal reflux, erosive esophagitis, and hypersecretory conditions.

Short-term treatment of active duodenal ulcer and active benign gastric ulcer, maintenance therapy for duodenal ulcer, treatment of symptomatic nonerosive GERD and endoscopically diagnosed erosive esophagitis, and pathological hypersecretory conditions.
Common adverse reactions include headache, dizziness, constipation, and diarrhea.

Rare serious reactions include anaphylaxis, severe skin reactions, blood dyscrasias, hepatic injury, confusion or other CNS reactions, and arrhythmias including QT prolongation, especially with renal impairment.
Contraindicated in patients with serious hypersensitivity to famotidine or other H2-receptor antagonists.
A symptomatic response does not exclude gastric malignancy; evaluate persistent or recurrent symptoms appropriately.
Use lower doses or longer intervals in moderate or severe renal impairment to reduce CNS adverse reactions and QT prolongation risk.
The elimination half-life is approximately 2.5 to 3.5 hours in patients with normal renal function and is prolonged in renal impairment.
Famotidine is eliminated substantially by the kidney, including active tubular secretion.
By raising gastric pH, famotidine can reduce absorption of drugs whose bioavailability depends on an acidic environment; review product-specific interaction guidance.
Famotidine may substantially increase tizanidine concentrations, causing hypotension, bradycardia, or excessive drowsiness; avoid concomitant use if possible and monitor closely if it is necessary.
Monitor symptom response, alarm features, renal function for dose selection, and new CNS or rhythm symptoms in susceptible patients.
Dose adjustment is required for creatinine clearance below the label threshold because exposure and half-life increase.
Select geriatric doses cautiously according to renal function rather than age alone.
Overdose management is supportive, with clinical monitoring and removal of unabsorbed drug when appropriate.
Famotidine is an H2-receptor antagonist that lowers gastric acid secretion; it is not a proton-pump inhibitor.
Renal elimination makes dose adjustment and CNS/QT surveillance important in renal impairment.

用於：逆轉BZD鎮靜或BZD過量（需慎選病人）。
考點：慢性BZD依賴或TCA混合中毒會誘發癲癇。
常考/禁忌：焦慮、躁動、噁心；癲癇、急性戒斷、再鎮靜。

statements.text: Flumazenil competitively antagonizes benzodiazepine activity at the benzodiazepine recognition site on the GABA-A receptor complex.
It reverses benzodiazepine-induced sedation and psychomotor impairment but does not reliably reverse effects of opioids, barbiturates, ethanol, or non-benzodiazepine mechanisms.

Flumazenil can improve alertness after benzodiazepine sedation, but it has not been established as an effective treatment for benzodiazepine-induced hypoventilation; resedation can recur when its effect wears off before the benzodiazepine effect.
Complete or partial reversal of sedative effects of benzodiazepines used for conscious sedation or general anesthesia.
Management of suspected benzodiazepine overdose in adults.
Common reactions include dizziness, injection-site pain, sweating, headache, abnormal vision, nausea, vomiting, and agitation.

Seizures are the major serious risk, especially in physically dependent patients, mixed cyclic-antidepressant overdose, patients treated with benzodiazepines for seizure control, or those with seizure predisposition.

Contraindicated in serious hypersensitivity to flumazenil or benzodiazepines, when a benzodiazepine was administered for a potentially life-threatening condition such as status epilepticus or intracranial-pressure control, and in serious cyclic-antidepressant overdose signs.
Flumazenil does not replace airway management, ventilation, circulatory support, and careful observation in overdose or procedural recovery.
Monitor for resedation, respiratory depression, withdrawal, agitation, and seizures after the initial response.
Reversal generally begins within 1 to 2 minutes after intravenous administration, with peak response commonly within several minutes.
The terminal half-life is approximately 40 to 80 minutes in healthy adults.
Flumazenil is extensively metabolized in the liver to inactive metabolites.
Its clinically important interaction context is mixed overdose: reversal of protective benzodiazepine effects can unmask seizures or dysrhythmia from cyclic antidepressants and other proconvulsants.
Continuously assess airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness, resedation, withdrawal, and seizures for an observation period appropriate to the benzodiazepine and coingestants.
Clearance is reduced and half-life prolonged in hepatic impairment; repeat dosing should be titrated cautiously.
Pediatric evidence is limited to reversal of conscious sedation in patients older than 1 year; safety in pediatric overdose is not established.
Excess flumazenil exposure is generally managed supportively, but abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal and seizures remain the key hazards.
Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine-site antagonist and does not reverse opioid effects.

Do not use flumazenil reflexively in serious mixed overdose or benzodiazepine dependence: reversal can precipitate seizures, especially with cyclic-antidepressant toxicity or another seizure predisposition.

items.text: Ketamine：靶點：NMDA receptor。機轉：非競爭性NMDA拮抗 → 解離性麻醉、止痛、支氣管擴張；也增加交感活性。
用於：麻醉誘導/短程程序鎮靜、疼痛、治療抗性憂鬱（特定劑型）。
一句話：Ketamine = NMDA antagonist + dissociative anesthesia。
常考：幻覺/甦醒反應、流涎、血壓心跳上升、顱內壓疑慮、濫用與膀胱炎。

statements.text: Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia primarily through noncompetitive antagonism of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor, with additional effects at other receptor and ion-channel systems.
Ketamine produces profound analgesia, amnesia, and cataleptic dissociation while commonly increasing blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output through sympathetic stimulation.
The reviewed injectable product produces rapid dissociative general anesthesia and can be used alone for suitable procedures, for induction, or as a supplement to other anesthetic agents.
Sole anesthetic agent for diagnostic and surgical procedures that do not require skeletal-muscle relaxation.
Induction of anesthesia before other general anesthetic agents and supplementation of low-potency anesthetic agents.
Common reactions include increased blood pressure and pulse, nausea, vomiting, increased secretions, nystagmus, diplopia, and emergence phenomena such as vivid dreams or delirium.

Serious risks include respiratory depression or apnea, laryngospasm and airway obstruction, marked hemodynamic instability, severe emergence reactions, anaphylaxis, drug-induced liver injury with recurrent dosing, and serious urologic complications with long-term use or abuse.
Recurrent or prolonged use has been associated with hepatobiliary dysfunction and ketamine-induced cystitis or urinary tract injury.
Ketamine is contraindicated when a significant elevation of blood pressure would constitute a serious hazard and in patients with hypersensitivity to ketamine or excipients.
Only clinicians experienced in general anesthesia and airway management should administer ketamine, with resuscitative equipment immediately available.

Protect the airway and monitor ventilation even though spontaneous respiration and airway reflexes may be relatively preserved; rapid administration or excessive dose can cause respiratory depression.
Minimize emergence reactions with a calm recovery environment and appropriate adjuncts when clinically indicated.
Ketamine has abuse and dependence potential; secure handling and assess repeated-use complications.

Repeated or prolonged exposure to anesthetic or sedative drugs during early brain development may pose neurodevelopmental risk; for elective procedures in young children, weigh the benefits against exposure duration and timing.
statements.scope: Pediatric neurotoxicity warning; clinical significance of the nonclinical findings remains uncertain

statements.text: For recurrent ketamine dosing, obtain baseline and periodic liver-function tests; discontinue and refer for evaluation if findings suggest sclerosing cholangitis or other clinically important hepatobiliary injury.

Long-term ketamine use or abuse can cause cystitis, reduced bladder capacity, ureteral stenosis or obstruction, and hydronephrosis; discontinue and seek urgent urologic evaluation for obstruction or severe lower-urinary-tract symptoms.
Ketamine has been associated with increased intracranial pressure; patients with elevated intracranial pressure require a monitored setting and frequent neurologic assessments.
After IV administration, surgical anesthesia generally occurs within about 30 seconds; after IM administration, onset is usually within several minutes.
A single IV dose usually provides several minutes of surgical anesthesia, while IM administration generally lasts longer; recovery may be prolonged by repeat dosing.
Ketamine is hepatically metabolized, principally through CYP pathways to norketamine and other metabolites.
Metabolites are eliminated mainly in urine.
Opioids, benzodiazepines, and other CNS depressants can increase profound sedation and respiratory depression.
Sympathomimetics and vasopressin may enhance ketamine's sympathomimetic effects; closely monitor vital signs and individualize dose adjustment during concomitant use.
Theophylline or aminophylline with ketamine may lower the seizure threshold; use an alternative to ketamine when possible.

Continuously monitor airway patency, oxygenation, ventilation, blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, anesthetic depth, and recovery behavior; for recurrent dosing obtain baseline and periodic liver tests and assess urinary symptoms, and perform frequent neurologic assessments when intracranial pressure is elevated.
Use in pregnancy requires benefit-risk assessment; safety for obstetric anesthesia has not been established except for limited studied contexts.
Pediatric dosing is weight-based and requires the same airway, cardiovascular, and recovery safeguards as adult anesthesia.

Repeated or prolonged anesthesia or sedation exposure in children younger than 3 years may adversely affect the developing brain; discuss the benefits, risks, timing, and duration of elective procedures with caregivers.

Overdose or excessively rapid administration can cause prolonged anesthesia, respiratory depression, apnea, cardiovascular instability, and emergence reactions; provide ventilatory and supportive care.
Ketamine is the classic dissociative anesthetic and NMDA-receptor antagonist; it often raises rather than lowers blood pressure and heart rate.
Preserved spontaneous breathing does not mean the airway is guaranteed: laryngospasm, obstruction, apnea, and aspiration risk still require full monitoring.

items.text: Lapatinib：靶點：HER2/EGFR tyrosine kinase。機轉：小分子TKI阻斷HER2/EGFR訊號 → 腫瘤增殖下降。
用於：HER2陽性乳癌等。
一句話：Lapatinib = HER2/EGFR TKI。
常考：腹瀉、皮疹、肝毒性、心肌功能下降；避免強CYP3A4交互作用。

mnemonics.text: p.93: 帶孫子(台，Trastu)怕吐(pertu-)，就吸HER懶趴(lapa-)
p.93: 她(HER)抓著(Trastu-)、捧著(Pertuzu-)我的大懶趴(lapa-)

statements.text: Lapatinib is a small-molecule reversible inhibitor of the intracellular tyrosine-kinase domains of EGFR (ErbB1) and HER2 (ErbB2), reducing downstream proliferative signaling.
Inhibition of EGFR/HER2 signaling suppresses growth of tumors driven by HER2; clinical activity depends on the labeled tumor and combination regimen.
Lapatinib is used in combination regimens for selected HER2-positive advanced or metastatic breast-cancer populations.

In combination with capecitabine for selected patients with advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer whose disease has progressed after prior therapy including an anthracycline, a taxane, and trastuzumab.
In combination with letrozole for postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer for whom hormonal therapy is indicated.
Common adverse reactions include diarrhea, rash, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia with capecitabine, and nail or skin disorders.

Serious risks include hepatotoxicity, decreased left-ventricular ejection fraction, QT prolongation, severe diarrhea with dehydration, interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis, and severe cutaneous reactions.
Boxed warning: hepatotoxicity has occurred, including rare deaths; monitor liver function and discontinue permanently for severe changes as directed.
Lapatinib is contraindicated in patients with known severe hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, to the product or any component.
Assess left-ventricular ejection fraction before treatment and during therapy; interrupt or discontinue for clinically important decline.
Treat diarrhea promptly, correct fluid and electrolyte deficits, and interrupt treatment for severe or persistent toxicity.
Use caution in patients with QT-risk factors and correct hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia before treatment.
The effective half-life after repeated dosing is about 24 hours, with accumulation during once-daily administration.
Lapatinib is extensively metabolized, mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5, and also inhibits or interacts with several transporters and CYP pathways.
Food markedly increases and variably changes lapatinib exposure; the labeled dose is taken consistently at least one hour before or one hour after a meal.
Strong CYP3A inhibitors increase lapatinib exposure and strong CYP3A inducers decrease it; the label provides avoidance or dose-modification guidance.

Use caution and consider reducing the concomitant drug dose when lapatinib is given with narrow-therapeutic-window substrates of CYP3A4, CYP2C8, or P-glycoprotein; BCRP inhibition is described only in vitro and is not included in this clinical substrate guidance.

Lapatinib increased oral digoxin exposure about 2.8-fold; monitor serum digoxin before starting lapatinib and throughout coadministration, and follow the label's digoxin dose-reduction instruction when the concentration exceeds its threshold.
Avoid or carefully manage other QT-prolonging drugs and agents that disturb electrolytes.

Monitor liver tests before treatment and at label-specified intervals, LVEF, diarrhea and hydration, pulmonary symptoms, skin toxicity, ECG and electrolytes in at-risk patients, and medication interactions.
Lapatinib can cause fetal harm; verify pregnancy status when appropriate and use effective contraception during treatment and for the label-specified interval afterward.

statements.text: Nizatidine is a competitive, reversible inhibitor of histamine at H2 receptors, particularly those on gastric parietal cells.
Nizatidine inhibits nocturnal and food-, caffeine-, betazole-, and pentagastrin-stimulated gastric acid secretion; total pepsin output falls in proportion to the reduced volume of gastric secretion.

Clinical trials and the labeled indications support healing of active duodenal and benign gastric ulcers, maintenance after duodenal-ulcer healing, and treatment of GERD with endoscopically diagnosed esophagitis.

The capsule label includes short-term treatment of active duodenal ulcer, maintenance after healing of duodenal ulcer, treatment of endoscopically diagnosed esophagitis and associated heartburn due to GERD, and short-term treatment of active benign gastric ulcer.

Treatment-emergent events reported in at least 1% of nizatidine-treated trial participants included headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, and other gastrointestinal or nervous-system symptoms; several occurred at similar or higher rates with placebo.

Clinically important reported reactions include hepatic injury with hepatitis or jaundice, reversible confusion, thrombocytopenia, vasculitis, anaphylaxis or other hypersensitivity reactions, and serum-sickness-like reactions.

Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to nizatidine; because class cross-sensitivity has been observed, H2-receptor antagonists should not be given to patients with a history of hypersensitivity to another H2-receptor antagonist.
A symptomatic response does not exclude gastric malignancy, and benign gastric ulceration should be distinguished from malignant disease before therapy.
Because nizatidine is excreted primarily by the kidney, reduce the amount and/or frequency of dosing in moderate to severe renal insufficiency according to creatinine clearance.
The elimination half-life is 1 to 2 hours with normal renal function and is prolonged in moderate to severe renal impairment.
More than 90% of an oral dose is excreted in urine within 12 hours, about 60% as unchanged nizatidine; active tubular secretion contributes to renal clearance.

The label reports no observed interactions with theophylline, chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam, lidocaine, phenytoin, or warfarin and no inhibition of the cytochrome P450-linked drug-metabolizing system; very high-dose aspirin increased serum salicylate concentrations during concomitant nizatidine.
Monitor symptom response and alarm features, renal function for dose selection, and clinically important hepatic, hematologic, hypersensitivity, or CNS reactions.
The label reports no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women and recommends use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.

About 0.1% of an administered oral dose was secreted in human milk; the label advises deciding whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue nizatidine, considering the drug's importance to the mother.
Moderate to severe renal impairment prolongs half-life and lowers clearance; reduce dose amount and/or frequency according to renal function to avoid accumulation.
In patients with normal renal function and uncomplicated hepatic dysfunction, nizatidine disposition was similar to that in subjects without hepatic dysfunction; hepatorenal syndrome was not studied.
Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established.
Older adults did not show overall safety or effectiveness differences in trials, but renal function should guide dose selection because nizatidine is substantially excreted by the kidney.

Human overdose experience is limited; management consists of clinical monitoring and supportive care, and nizatidine is not expected to be efficiently removed by hemodialysis because of its large volume of distribution.
Nizatidine is a competitive, reversible H2-receptor antagonist with substantial renal elimination and a 1-to-2-hour elimination half-life in normal renal function.

Do not transfer cimetidine-specific endocrine or CYP-inhibition effects to nizatidine: this label reports no demonstrable antiandrogenic action and no inhibition of the cytochrome P450-linked drug-metabolizing system.

statements.text: Oxybutynin relaxes bladder smooth muscle through a direct antispasmodic effect and inhibition of acetylcholine's muscarinic action on smooth muscle.

Treatment of overactive bladder with urge urinary incontinence, urgency, and frequency in adults.
Treatment of symptoms of detrusor overactivity associated with a neurologic condition in pediatric patients 6 years and older.

Clinically important reactions and risks include angioedema or anaphylaxis, central anticholinergic effects, urinary or gastric retention, worsening gastrointestinal motility, glaucoma, arrhythmia, tachycardia, and QT prolongation.
Contraindications include urinary retention, gastric retention or severe decreased gastrointestinal motility, uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma, and hypersensitivity.
Stop immediately and treat if angioedema threatens the airway.
Monitor for hallucinations, agitation, confusion, somnolence, and other CNS anticholinergic effects, especially after starting or increasing the dose.

Anticholinergic suppression of sweating can contribute to heat prostration in high environmental temperatures.
Oxybutynin is extensively metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, including N-desethyloxybutynin.
The extended-release tablet is designed for once-daily administration and must be swallowed whole; it must not be crushed, divided, or chewed.
Other anticholinergic drugs can add to dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, somnolence, and urinary retention.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors increase oxybutynin exposure and may increase toxicity.
Monitor urgency and incontinence response, post-void or retention symptoms, bowel function, mental status, ocular symptoms, heat intolerance, and additive anticholinergic burden.
There are no adequate data in pregnant women to evaluate a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes.
There are no data on oxybutynin in human milk, effects on the breastfed infant, or effects on milk production; weigh breastfeeding benefits, the mother's clinical need, and potential infant effects.
The selected label reports no dedicated renal-impairment studies; use requires individualized caution.
The selected label reports no dedicated hepatic-impairment studies; use requires individualized caution.
Extended-release tablets are labeled for selected patients 6 years and older who can swallow the tablet whole; use below age 6 is not recommended.

Overdose has been associated with CNS excitation, flushing, fever, dehydration, cardiac arrhythmia, vomiting, and urinary retention; account for continued extended-release absorption, monitor for at least 24 hours, and provide symptomatic supportive care.
Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic drug for overactive bladder; expected adverse effects are dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, cognitive effects, and urinary retention.
Do not use in urinary or gastric retention or uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma.

items.text: Prednisone：活化細胞內glucocorticoid receptor → 改變基因轉錄；抑制PLA2/COX-2、降低細胞激素與免疫反應。

statements.text: Prednisone is completely converted to active prednisolone; the selected label describes potent anti-inflammatory corticosteroid effects, modification of immune responses, and varied metabolic effects.
Glucocorticoid effects include anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive activity together with metabolic, mineral, bone, neuropsychiatric, endocrine, and cardiovascular effects.
Systemic prednisone reduces inflammation and immune activity across many labeled disorders, including acute inflammatory bowel disease exacerbations.
The selected systemic prednisone label includes acute exacerbations of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis among its gastrointestinal indications.

The label also includes numerous allergic, dermatologic, endocrine, hematologic, neoplastic, neurologic, ophthalmic, renal, respiratory, and rheumatologic conditions requiring systemic glucocorticoid therapy.
Dose- and duration-related effects include increased appetite, weight gain, fluid retention, hypertension, hyperglycemia, dyspepsia, insomnia, mood change, acne, and bruising.

Serious toxicities include severe or opportunistic infection, adrenal suppression and withdrawal crisis, osteoporosis and fractures, avascular necrosis, gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, psychosis, cataract or glaucoma, and thromboembolic or cardiovascular complications.
Live or live-attenuated vaccines can cause disseminated infection during immunosuppressive glucocorticoid dosing.
Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to prednisone or any excipient in the formulation.
Use the lowest effective dose and taper after prolonged or high-dose therapy to reduce adrenal-insufficiency risk; stress dosing may be required during illness or surgery.

Screen for and monitor infection. Systemic fungal infection is an avoid-use warning with an exception when prednisone is needed to control a drug reaction; it is not listed as a section 4 contraindication in this product label.
Do not administer live or live-attenuated vaccines to patients receiving immunosuppressive corticosteroid doses.
Monitor for hypertension, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, hyperglycemia, psychiatric symptoms, ocular toxicity, osteoporosis, myopathy, gastrointestinal complications, and growth suppression.
The delayed-release tablet releases prednisone approximately four hours after ingestion, so administration timing is intentionally different from immediate-release products.

Prednisone is rapidly converted to prednisolone, which is further metabolized hepatically before renal excretion of metabolites.
CYP3A inhibitors may increase and CYP3A inducers may decrease systemic glucocorticoid exposure.
NSAIDs, anticoagulants, potassium-depleting agents, antidiabetic drugs, immunosuppressants, and vaccines require individualized monitoring or avoidance.

Use in pregnancy requires maternal-fetal benefit-risk assessment; prolonged or repeated exposure may affect fetal growth and neonatal adrenal function.
Prednisolone appears in human milk; consider dose, timing, treatment duration, and infant exposure when breastfeeding.
The effects of hepatic impairment on prednisone or prednisolone pharmacokinetics after the selected delayed-release product have not been evaluated.
Children are more susceptible to growth suppression and other systemic corticosteroid effects; use the lowest effective exposure and monitor growth.
Acute overdose is generally managed supportively, whereas chronic excess produces Cushingoid features, metabolic complications, infection risk, osteoporosis, and HPA-axis suppression.
Prednisone is completely converted to active prednisolone; the selected delayed-release tablet begins releasing prednisone about four hours after intake.

Long-term or high-dose therapy must be tapered because systemic corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis.

Sorafenib undergoes oxidative metabolism by hepatic CYP3A4 and glucuronidation by UGT1A9.
Most administered radioactivity is recovered in feces, with a smaller fraction in urine as glucuronidated metabolites.

In vitro, sorafenib inhibits UGT1A1, UGT1A9, and P-glycoprotein and could increase exposure or concentrations of their substrates; this is mechanistic interaction evidence rather than a quantified clinical dosing rule.

No dose adjustment is generally required for renal impairment not requiring dialysis; dialysis patients were not studied.
Mild or moderate hepatic impairment generally does not require dose adjustment, but severe hepatic impairment has not been adequately studied.

statements.text: Topiramate blocks voltage-dependent sodium channels, enhances GABA activity at some GABA-A receptor subtypes, antagonizes AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors, and weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase isozymes II and IV.

The combined sodium-channel, GABAergic, glutamatergic, and carbonic-anhydrase effects contribute to antiseizure and migraine-preventive activity, although the precise clinical mechanism is not fully defined.
Topiramate reduces seizure frequency in labeled epilepsies and prevents migraine; weight loss is a frequent pharmacologic effect but is not a standalone indication of the reviewed TOPAMAX products.

Preventive treatment of migraine in patients 12 years of age and older.
Common dose-related reactions include paresthesia, cognitive slowing, attention or memory difficulty, language problems, fatigue, somnolence, dizziness, taste alteration, anorexia, and weight loss.

Concomitant valproate can be associated with hyperammonemia or encephalopathy and with hypothermia, with or without hyperammonemia.

Measure serum bicarbonate at baseline and periodically; consider dose reduction or discontinuation for persistent metabolic acidosis.
Counsel about urgent eye pain or visual change, reduced sweating or fever, cognitive and mood effects, serious hypersensitivity or skin reactions, kidney-stone prevention, and fetal risk.
Withdraw TOPAMAX gradually to minimize the potential for seizures or increased seizure frequency, including in patients without a seizure history.
Peak plasma concentration occurs approximately 2 hours after an immediate-release oral dose.
The mean elimination half-life is about 21 hours in patients with normal renal function.
Topiramate is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine; clearance falls in renal impairment and it is removed by hemodialysis.

Valproate increases hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and hypothermia risk; other carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors and therapies that promote metabolic acidosis, including a ketogenic diet, increase acidosis and kidney-stone risk.
Topiramate can decrease contraceptive efficacy and increase breakthrough bleeding, especially above 200 mg/day; counsel patients using contraceptives.
Use extreme caution with alcohol or other CNS depressants because concomitant administration has not been evaluated and may add cognitive or neuropsychiatric effects.
Monitor seizure or migraine response, serum bicarbonate, renal function, hydration and stone symptoms, weight and growth, cognition, mood/suicidality, ocular symptoms, and pregnancy risk.
Topiramate exposure in pregnancy increases risks including oral clefts and small-for-gestational-age birth; counsel patients who can become pregnant and consider alternative therapy when appropriate.

Topiramate is excreted in human milk; milk-production effects are unknown, and diarrhea and somnolence have been reported in breastfed infants. Weigh breastfeeding benefits, the mother's clinical need, and potential infant effects.
Use approximately one-half the usual adult dose when creatinine clearance is below 70 mL/min/1.73 m² and supplement dosing around hemodialysis as directed.
Plasma clearance of topiramate decreased by a mean of 26% in patients with moderate to severe hepatic impairment.
Pediatric use is indication- and age-specific; monitor growth, weight, bicarbonate, cognition, heat illness, and bone-related consequences of chronic acidosis.
Overdose can cause seizures, drowsiness, speech and vision disturbances, hypotension, severe metabolic acidosis, coma, and death; hemodialysis can enhance removal.
High-yield mechanism quartet: sodium-channel blockade, GABA-A enhancement, AMPA/kainate antagonism, and carbonic-anhydrase inhibition.
Classic adverse-effect cluster: paresthesia, cognitive slowing, weight loss, metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, oligohidrosis, and angle-closure glaucoma.
The weight-management product is a phentermine/topiramate fixed combination; do not relabel single-agent TOPAMAX as an approved obesity drug.

statements.text: Phytonadione (vitamin K1) supplies vitamin K needed by the liver to produce active coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Phytonadione corrects vitamin-K-responsive coagulopathy and prevents or treats vitamin K deficiency bleeding in neonates.

Coagulation disorders due to faulty formation of vitamin-K-dependent factors when caused by vitamin K deficiency or interference with vitamin K activity, including coumarin-anticoagulant and selected non-anticoagulant causes.
Prophylaxis and treatment of vitamin K deficiency bleeding in neonates.

Fatal or severe anaphylaxis, shock, cardiorespiratory arrest, hypotension, dyspnea, and cyanosis have occurred with IV or IM administration, including on first exposure and despite dilution.

statements.text: Boxed warning: fatal hypersensitivity reactions have occurred during and immediately after IV and IM phytonadione injection; avoid these routes unless subcutaneous administration is not feasible and the risk is justified.

Use subcutaneous administration whenever possible; if IV use is unavoidable, inject very slowly and be prepared to manage anaphylaxis.
Use benzyl-alcohol-free phytonadione in neonates and infants when available.
Vitamin K1 is not itself a clotting factor and may not adequately correct bleeding caused by severe liver failure or non-vitamin-K-responsive coagulopathy.
Improvement in INR may begin within 1 to 8 hours after injection, so interim blood or clotting-component therapy may be necessary for severe bleeding.
The product is light sensitive and route selection matters: subcutaneous administration is preferred whenever feasible because IV and IM administration carry serious hypersensitivity risk.
Large phytonadione doses can produce temporary resistance to vitamin-K-antagonist anticoagulants; phytonadione does not reverse heparin anticoagulation.
Monitor INR before and after administration and reassess after the label-specified interval; monitor for hypersensitivity during parenteral dosing and for thromboembolic risk from overcorrection.
Published human data have not shown a clear association with adverse developmental outcomes, but preservative exposure and the maternal bleeding indication require individualized assessment.
Phytonadione is present in human milk; a preservative-free formulation is preferred when available during lactation.
The aluminum content of prolonged parenteral products can accumulate in impaired renal function; premature neonates are particularly susceptible.
Efficacy for neonatal prophylaxis and treatment is established, but preservative-free formulations are preferred because of benzyl-alcohol toxicity risk.
Vitamin K1 Injection overdose can cause hemolysis, jaundice, and hyperbilirubinemia in newborns, particularly in premature infants.
For this phytonadione injection record, the cited U.S. label directly identifies factors II, VII, IX, and X as the vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors restored by treatment.
Phytonadione does not normalize anticoagulation immediately; severe bleeding may require clotting-factor replacement while vitamin K takes effect.

statements.text: Bretylium is taken up by peripheral adrenergic neurons. Archived labeling describes an initial release of norepinephrine followed by inhibition of norepinephrine release, producing peripheral adrenergic-neuron blockade.
Its historical antiarrhythmic action includes prolongation of myocardial action-potential duration and effective refractory period, consistent with its class III teaching classification.
The early norepinephrine-release phase can transiently increase blood pressure or ventricular ectopy; the subsequent adrenergic-neuron blockade can cause marked postural hypotension.

statements.text: The most clinically important historical toxicity is hypotension, especially postural hypotension; transient hypertension, bradycardia or ventricular ectopy can occur during the initial catecholamine-release phase.

The archived U.S. label states that there were no contraindications for ventricular fibrillation or life-threatening refractory ventricular arrhythmias except arrhythmias caused by digitalis toxicity; do not use bretylium when digitalis is the suspected cause.

Keep patients supine during parenteral treatment and monitor closely for postural hypotension; volume depletion, fixed-cardiac-output states, and severe aortic stenosis can make hypotension especially hazardous.
Monitor for transient hypertension or worsening ventricular arrhythmia during the initial catecholamine-release phase and for hyperthermia during treatment.
The archived label reports an elimination half-life of approximately 6 to 10 hours in patients with normal renal function, with prolongation in renal impairment.
Approximately 70% to 80% of an administered dose is excreted unchanged in urine during the first 24 hours, and bretylium can be removed by hemodialysis.
Digitalis glycosides can aggravate ventricular ectopy during bretylium's initial catecholamine-release phase; concomitant therapy requires close rhythm monitoring.
Catecholamines can produce exaggerated pressor responses after adrenergic-neuron blockade, and monoamine-oxidase inhibitors may further intensify catecholamine effects.
Historical intravenous use required continuous ECG and frequent blood-pressure, perfusion, temperature, renal-function, and recurrent ventricular-arrhythmia assessment.

Excess exposure can produce profound hypotension and bradycardia. Management in the archived label is supportive, with supine positioning, intravenous fluids and vasopressor support when required; hemodialysis can remove bretylium.

Bretylium is retained as a historical Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic used for ventricular fibrillation and refractory ventricular tachycardia; this exam association is separate from present market availability and guideline preference.
Its biphasic adrenergic-neuron action explains both transient early catecholamine effects and the later, prominent postural hypotension.

statements.text: Clarithromycin is a macrolide antibacterial that binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible bacteria and inhibits protein synthesis.

Its antibacterial effect depends on organism susceptibility and exposure; resistance may involve ribosomal target modification, active efflux, or enzymatic drug inactivation, with cross-resistance possible among macrolides.
Clarithromycin treats selected susceptible respiratory, skin, otic, and mycobacterial infections and is used only in combination regimens for H. pylori eradication.

Labeled indications include selected mild-to-moderate bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, acute maxillary sinusitis, community-acquired pneumonia, pharyngitis or tonsillitis, uncomplicated skin infections, pediatric acute otitis media, and treatment or prophylaxis of disseminated MAC in advanced HIV.

For H. pylori infection and duodenal-ulcer disease, clarithromycin is labeled as part of specific combination regimens with a proton-pump inhibitor and usually amoxicillin; clarithromycin monotherapy is not the reviewed eradication strategy.
The most frequent adverse reactions are abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and dysgeusia.

Serious risks include QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, hepatotoxicity, severe cutaneous or systemic hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, and severe interaction-mediated toxicity.

The label describes an observed long-term all-cause mortality signal after clarithromycin exposure in patients with coronary artery disease; prescribers should weigh this risk and consider alternatives when appropriate.

Contraindications include macrolide hypersensitivity; prior clarithromycin-associated cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction; and specified high-risk combinations including cisapride, pimozide, ergot alkaloids, lomitapide, lovastatin, simvastatin, and lurasidone.
Concomitant colchicine is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment because clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A and P-glycoprotein and can cause fatal colchicine toxicity.
Avoid clarithromycin in patients with known QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, significant bradycardia, or concurrent class IA or III antiarrhythmics.
Discontinue for hepatitis symptoms or severe hypersensitivity; evaluate significant diarrhea for C. difficile infection and monitor for worsening myasthenia gravis.

Use antibacterial stewardship: treat only infections proven or strongly suspected to involve susceptible bacteria, and do not use clarithromycin-containing H. pylori regimens when resistance is known or suspected.
For current H. pylori treatment selection, the 2024 ACG guideline advises avoiding clarithromycin-containing regimens unless clarithromycin susceptibility has been demonstrated.
statements.scope: Current U.S. guideline; separate from product-label approval

statements.text: Clarithromycin and its active 14-hydroxy metabolite have dose- and regimen-dependent half-lives; accumulation and exposure increase when renal function is reduced.

Clarithromycin is metabolized in the liver, including CYP3A-mediated formation of the microbiologically active 14-hydroxy metabolite, and it is itself a clinically important CYP3A and P-glycoprotein inhibitor.
Renal elimination contributes substantially to clearance of clarithromycin and metabolites, so dosage reduction is required in severe renal impairment and in some interacting-drug settings.
Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A and P-glycoprotein and can markedly increase exposure to numerous substrates; contraindicated and dose-adjusted combinations must be checked individually.

Clinically important examples include statins, colchicine, calcium-channel blockers, carbamazepine, quetiapine, benzodiazepines, calcineurin inhibitors, anticoagulants, hypoglycemic agents, digoxin-like P-glycoprotein substrates, and QT-prolonging drugs.

Monitor clinical and microbiologic response, renal and hepatic function when relevant, ECG and electrolytes in patients at arrhythmic risk, and drug concentrations or toxicity for narrow-therapeutic-index interacting medicines.
Based on animal findings, the label advises against use during pregnancy unless no appropriate alternative exists and the potential benefit justifies fetal risk.
Clarithromycin and its active metabolite are present in human milk; weigh treatment need against potential infant gastrointestinal effects and altered flora.
Reduce dosage in severe renal impairment and apply additional reductions for specified interacting antiretroviral regimens.

No routine adjustment is required for hepatic impairment with normal renal function, but combined hepatic and renal dysfunction can increase exposure and prior clarithromycin-associated hepatic injury is a contraindication.
The label includes pediatric dosing for selected infections and MAC, while indication and formulation must be matched to age and weight.
Older adults may have greater exposure from renal impairment and a higher risk of QT-related arrhythmia, including torsades de pointes.

Overdose usually produces gastrointestinal symptoms and may worsen hepatic, neurologic, or interaction-related toxicity; remove unabsorbed drug and provide supportive care because hemodialysis does not meaningfully enhance elimination.
Clarithromycin is a macrolide 50S inhibitor and a potent interaction-prone CYP3A/P-glycoprotein inhibitor; QT prolongation and cholestatic or hepatocellular injury are classic safety clues.

Clarithromycin's U.S. label includes specified H. pylori combination regimens, but the 2024 ACG guideline advises against clarithromycin-containing treatment unless susceptibility is demonstrated; do not present clarithromycin as empiric monotherapy or an automatic first-line choice.

statements.text: Demeclocycline is a primarily bacteriostatic tetracycline antibacterial that is thought to inhibit susceptible bacterial protein synthesis.

Its approved clinical role in the selected label is treatment of infections caused by susceptible organisms, not diuresis or routine hyponatremia management.

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus has historically been exploited off-label to reduce water retention in SIADH, but the selected European hyponatremia guideline recommends against demeclocycline for moderate or profound SIADH because of limited benefit evidence and toxicity concerns.

Serious toxicities include renal failure and dose-related azotemia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hepatotoxicity, severe skin reactions, intracranial hypertension, C. difficile-associated diarrhea, blood dyscrasias, and anaphylaxis.
Use during tooth development can cause permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia; tetracyclines can also impair fetal skeletal development.

Monitor infection response, renal and hepatic function during prolonged therapy, hydration, symptoms of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, photosensitivity, intracranial-hypertension symptoms, and superinfection.
Tetracyclines cross the placenta and can affect fetal teeth and bone; demeclocycline should generally be avoided in pregnancy.

Tetracyclines are excreted in human milk; because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, decide whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue demeclocycline according to the drug's importance to the mother.
Reduce dose or extend dosing interval in renal impairment and monitor for accumulation, azotemia, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Overdose is treated by discontinuation and supportive care; tetracyclines are not removed in significant quantities by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.

Demeclocycline can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which underlies its historical off-label SIADH association; however, the cited European guideline recommends against demeclocycline for moderate or profound SIADH.

statements.text: The current injection label states that the precise mode of action is not known and describes a depressant action on hyperstimulated labyrinthine function.
CDC Yellow Book classifies dimenhydrinate among centrally acting H1 antihistamines used against motion sickness.
Its central anti-motion-sickness activity is accompanied by drowsiness and clinically relevant anticholinergic effects.
Parenteral dimenhydrinate prevents and treats nausea, vomiting, or vertigo associated with motion sickness when oral therapy is impractical.
Prevention and treatment of nausea, vomiting, or vertigo of motion sickness.
Drowsiness is the most frequent reaction; dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, difficult or painful urination, tachycardia, epigastric distress, excitation, and other listed reactions can occur.
Massive overdose can cause convulsions, coma, respiratory depression, or death; pediatric patients can also develop hallucinations or paradoxical excitation.
The injectable product contains benzyl alcohol; the label warns of fatal gasping syndrome in premature infants and infants of low birth weight.
Contraindicated in neonates and in patients with hypersensitivity to dimenhydrinate or its components, diphenhydramine or 8-chlorotheophylline.
Drowsiness can impair driving or hazardous activities; alcohol and other central nervous system depressants can have additive effects.

Do not inject the preparation intra-arterially.
Alcohol and other central nervous system depressants can add to impairment and sedation.
Dimenhydrinate can mask ototoxic symptoms from certain antibiotics, potentially delaying recognition of irreversible injury.
During parenteral use, observe alertness, respiratory status, anticholinergic adverse effects, injection-route safety, and recovery before hazardous activities.

Animal studies did not show fetal harm and available clinical experience did not indicate increased abnormalities, but adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking; use only if clearly needed.
Safety during labor and delivery has not been established. Reports indicate that dimenhydrinate may have an oxytocic effect, so use caution when that effect is unwanted or could be detrimental.
Small amounts are excreted in breast milk; decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug according to the treatment benefit.
Do not use in neonates; children can develop diminished alertness or paradoxical excitation, and overdose can cause hallucinations, convulsions, or death.
Massive overdose can cause convulsions, coma, and respiratory depression; no specific antidote is identified, so treatment is supportive with ventilation and seizure control as needed.
Dimenhydrinate is a centrally acting H1 antihistamine used for motion sickness; sedation and anticholinergic effects are key limitations.
The selected injection label supports motion-sickness nausea, vomiting, and vertigo; it does not justify a blanket “all-cause antiemetic” indication.

statements.text: Methohexital is an ultra-short-acting barbiturate that depresses the central nervous system and produces hypnosis and anesthesia.
A rapid rise in brain concentration produces unconsciousness; redistribution away from the brain accounts for brief hypnosis after a single IV dose, while repeated doses prolong recovery.
Methohexital provides rapid IV induction and brief anesthesia or sedation in appropriately monitored procedures, with selected IM or rectal induction use in pediatric patients.
IV induction of anesthesia before other general anesthetic agents, IV anesthesia for short procedures, and supplementation of subpotent inhalational anesthetics in adults.
Rectal or IM induction of anesthesia in pediatric patients older than 1 month in the product-specific settings described by the label.
BREVITAL is often associated with hiccups, coughing, and/or muscle twitching; temporary hypotension and tachycardia can occur after induction.

Serious risks include apnea and respiratory depression, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, airway obstruction, severe hypotension, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, and tissue injury from extravasation or intra-arterial injection.
Barbiturates can precipitate an acute porphyria attack in susceptible patients.

Boxed warning: use BREVITAL only in hospital or ambulatory-care settings with continuous respiratory and cardiac monitoring, immediate access to resuscitative drugs and age- and size-appropriate ventilation and intubation equipment, and personnel skilled in airway management; a separate designated individual must continuously monitor deeply sedated patients.
Contraindicated when general anesthesia is contraindicated, in latent or manifest porphyria, and in patients with known hypersensitivity to barbiturates.
Only clinicians trained in anesthesia and airway management should administer methohexital; oxygen, ventilation, intubation, and resuscitation equipment must be immediately available.
Avoid intra-arterial administration and manage extravasation promptly because severe vascular and tissue injury can occur.
Use reduced doses in debilitated, elderly, hemodynamically unstable, or cardiorespiratory-compromised patients and when other CNS depressants are present.

Repeated or prolonged anesthetic and sedation exposure during periods of rapid brain development caused neuronal and oligodendrocyte loss in animal studies; the clinical significance is uncertain, so balance procedure timing and benefit against potential risk in late pregnancy and young children.
BREVITAL is a Schedule IV controlled substance and may be habit-forming.
IV induction usually occurs within about 30 seconds.
After a single IV induction dose, hypnosis is typically brief because of rapid redistribution; repeated or continuous dosing prolongs anesthesia and recovery.
Methohexital is metabolized in the liver by oxidation and demethylation.
Metabolites are eliminated mainly through the kidneys.
BREVITAL's CNS-depressant effect can be additive with other CNS depressants, including ethyl alcohol and propylene glycol.

Prior chronic administration of barbiturates or phenytoin may reduce BREVITAL effectiveness; barbiturates may also influence the metabolism of concomitant drugs including phenytoin, halothane, anticoagulants, corticosteroids, ethyl alcohol, and propylene-glycol-containing solutions.
Continuously monitor airway, ventilation, oxygenation, blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, depth of anesthesia, injection site, and recovery until protective reflexes and cognition are adequate.

There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; animal studies found no adverse developmental effects at the label-described exposures, while prolonged anesthetic or sedation exposure during peak brain development produced neuronal apoptosis in pregnant primates.
BREVITAL has been used for cesarean delivery and readily and rapidly crosses the placenta because of its solubility and lack of protein binding.
Use caution when BREVITAL is administered to a nursing woman.
Use methohexital cautiously in patients with impaired renal function; the label does not provide a specific renal dose-adjustment algorithm.
Use methohexital cautiously in hepatic impairment because the liver performs its demethylation and oxidation; severe hepatic dysfunction may favor selection of another induction agent.
The product label supports selected rectal or IM induction in patients older than 1 month, with strict concentration, dose, airway, and monitoring requirements.
Older or debilitated patients generally require lower doses because circulatory and respiratory depression may be greater.

Overdose causes prolonged unconsciousness, respiratory arrest, hypotension, hypothermia, and cardiovascular collapse; secure the airway, ventilate, support circulation, and provide intensive monitoring.
Methohexital is an ultra-short-acting IV barbiturate anesthetic with rapid onset and brief effect after a single dose because of redistribution.
Its legacy placement under sedative-hypnotics reflects barbiturate class membership, but the selected label supports anesthesia and procedural use rather than chronic anxiety treatment.
Porphyria is a true contraindication; immediate airway and resuscitation capability is a boxed-warning condition of safe administration, not an additional contraindication.
